rubric.point: Principle: photovoltaic effect in p–n junction
Construction with labelled diagram (thin n-layer, p-base, grid contacts, anti-reflection coating)
Materials used (Si, GaAs, CdTe, CIGS, etc.)
Working: absorption of photons hν ≥ E<sub>g</sub>, electron–hole pair generation, separation by junction field, photocurrent
I–V relation I = I<sub>L</sub> − I₀(e^{qV/kT} − 1) and 4th-quadrant characteristic with V<sub>oc</sub>, I<sub>sc</sub>
Maximum power point P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>I<sub>m</sub>, fill factor and efficiency

answer: Principle. A solar cell is a p–n junction device that converts light energy directly into electrical energy by the photovoltaic effect: generation of an emf across a junction when illuminated.

Construction. A thin n-type layer (≈ 0.3–0.5 μm) is diffused on a thicker p-type silicon wafer (≈ 300 μm) to form a p–n junction close to the top surface. The top surface has metallic finger/grid contacts (front electrode) that leave most area open for light; the back has a full metal contact. The top is coated with an anti-reflection coating (SiOx or Si3N4) to reduce reflection from ~30 % to < 5 %. The cell is encapsulated by glass.

Materials. Crystalline silicon (mono- and poly-crystalline, Eg = 1.1 eV, efficiency 15–22 %), amorphous silicon, GaAs (Eg = 1.43 eV, high efficiency, space use), CdTe, CIGS (thin film), perovskites and multi-junction cells.

Working. (1) In the junction a depletion region with a built-in electric field directed from n to p exists. (2) Photons of energy hν ≥ Eg are absorbed in or near the depletion region, generating electron–hole pairs. (3) The junction field sweeps electrons to the n-side and holes to the p-side (minority carriers generated within a diffusion length also reach the junction). (4) This charge separation creates a photo-voltage (open-circuit voltage) across the terminals, with n-side negative and p-side positive; when an external load is connected, a current flows from the p terminal through the load to n terminal. Photons with hν < Eg are not absorbed and those with hν > Eg waste the excess as heat.

I–V characteristic. The cell current is I = IL − I₀(eqV/ηkT − 1), where IL is the light-generated current (proportional to the illumination) and I₀ the reverse saturation current. The curve is the diode characteristic shifted down by IL, and so lies in the fourth quadrant (V positive, I negative from the diode convention) where the device delivers power.
Short-circuit current Isc (V = 0) = IL. Open-circuit voltage Voc (I = 0) = (ηkT/q) ln(1 + IL/I₀) (≈ 0.6 V for silicon).

Maximum power: the load for which the product VI is largest corresponds to the "knee" of the curve, Pmax = VmIm. The fill factor FF = VmIm/(VocIsc) (typically 0.7–0.85) and the efficiency η = Pmax/Pin = VocIscFF/Pin.

Second graph: I–V curve in the fourth quadrant, intersecting the voltage axis at V<sub>oc</sub> and the current axis at I<sub>sc</sub>, with the rectangle V<sub>m</sub>I<sub>m</sub> marked at the knee.

rubric.point: Principle: electroluminescence by radiative recombination in a forward-biased p–n junction
Construction (epitaxial layers, contacts, dome/reflector) with diagram and symbol
Materials: GaAs, GaAsP, GaP, GaN, InGaN with colours and λ = 1240/E<sub>g</sub>
Working with energy-band description (hν ≈ E<sub>g</sub>)
V–I characteristics (threshold/knee voltage, exponential rise, no light in reverse bias)
Why direct bandgap semiconductors are preferred

answer: Principle. An LED is a forward-biased p–n junction that emits light through electroluminescence: when electrons and holes injected across the junction recombine radiatively, the energy released is emitted as photons of energy hν ≈ Eg.

Construction. Heavily doped n-type and p-type layers of a compound semiconductor are grown epitaxially on a substrate (e.g. GaAs). A thin active region lies at the junction; the p-layer is kept thin so that the light can escape. The top metal contact is a small ring or dot, the bottom contact is the full-area metal. The chip is placed in a reflecting cup and enclosed in an epoxy dome, which acts as lens and improves light extraction. The longer lead is the anode.

Materials. Wavelength λ(nm) = 1240/Eg(eV). GaAs (Eg = 1.43 eV, infrared 870–950 nm); GaAs1−xPx (red/orange/yellow, 1.8–2.0 eV); GaP (green/red); AlGaInP (red–yellow); GaN and InGaN (blue, green, white with phosphor, 2.7–3.4 eV). Silicon and germanium are not used because they are indirect-gap materials.

Working. Under forward bias the potential barrier is lowered; electrons from n-side and holes from p-side are injected into the junction region where they become minority carriers in excess. They recombine, with an electron falling from the conduction band to the valence band emitting a photon hν = Ec − Ev ≈ Eg. The light intensity is proportional to the forward current.

V–I characteristics. For forward bias the current is negligible below the threshold (knee) voltage Vγ ≈ Eg/q (≈ 1.2 V for IR, 1.8–2.0 V for red, 2.1 V green, 3–3.5 V for blue/white); beyond it the current rises very rapidly (exponentially) and so a series resistor R = (Vs − VF)/IF must be used to limit the current. In reverse bias the current is very small and no light is emitted; the reverse breakdown voltage is low (~5 V). The characteristic is the usual diode curve shifted to higher knee voltage.

Why direct bandgap semiconductors? In a direct bandgap material (GaAs, GaN) the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum occur at the same crystal momentum k, so an electron can recombine with a hole without change of momentum and the whole energy emerges as a photon – high radiative recombination probability, hence high efficiency. In an indirect bandgap material (Si, Ge) the minima occur at different k; recombination requires the simultaneous emission or absorption of a phonon to conserve momentum, which is a much less probable (three-body) process, so most recombination is non-radiative (heat). Hence direct bandgap materials are preferred for LEDs and lasers.

rubric.point: Expression for electron concentration n = N<sub>c</sub> exp[−(E<sub>c</sub> − E<sub>F</sub>)/kT]
Expression for hole concentration p = N<sub>v</sub> exp[−(E<sub>F</sub> − E<sub>v</sub>)/kT]
Condition n = p = n<sub>i</sub> for intrinsic semiconductor
Solution E<sub>F</sub> = (E<sub>c</sub> + E<sub>v</sub>)/2 + (kT/2)ln(N<sub>v</sub>/N<sub>c</sub>) and the result with equal effective masses
Effect of temperature in intrinsic semiconductor (stays near mid-gap, shift 3kT/4 ln(m<sub>h</sub>/m<sub>e</sub>))
Effect of temperature in n-type and p-type (movement of E_F towards E<sub>i</sub>, formula)

answer: Carrier concentrations. In a non-degenerate semiconductor the density of electrons in the conduction band is n = Nc exp[−(Ec − EF)/kT] … (1) and the density of holes in the valence band is p = Nv exp[−(EF − Ev)/kT] … (2), where Nc = 2(2πme*kT/h²)3/2 and Nv = 2(2πmh*kT/h²)3/2.
Intrinsic semiconductor: every electron in the conduction band has come from the valence band, leaving a hole, so n = p = ni. … (3)
Equating (1) and (2): N<sub>c</sub> exp[−(E<sub>c</sub> − E<sub>F</sub>)/kT] = N<sub>v</sub> exp[−(E<sub>F</sub> − E<sub>v</sub>)/kT].

Taking logarithms: ln N<sub>c</sub> − (E<sub>c</sub> − E<sub>F</sub>)/kT = ln N<sub>v</sub> − (E<sub>F</sub> − E<sub>v</sub>)/kT ⇒ 2E<sub>F</sub>/kT = (E<sub>c</sub> + E<sub>v</sub>)/kT + ln(N<sub>v</sub>/N<sub>c</sub>).
Hence EF = (Ec + Ev)/2 + (kT/2) ln(Nv/Nc) = (Ec + Ev)/2 + (3kT/4) ln(mh*/me*). … (4)

If the effective masses of the electron and hole are equal (me* = mh*, Nc = Nv), the second term vanishes and EF = (Ec + Ev)/2: the Fermi level lies exactly in the middle of the forbidden gap. For real materials the second term is only a few percent of Eg (mh* slightly larger than me* gives a small upward shift), and EF remains close to mid-gap.

Temperature effects – intrinsic: from (4), EF is at the mid-gap at 0 K and changes only by the small term ∝ T (e.g., slightly up if mh* > me*), so EF stays in the middle of the gap. The carrier density ni = √(NcNv) exp(−Eg/2kT) rises rapidly with T.

Extrinsic – n-type: at T = 0 K, EF lies midway between the donor level Ed and Ec. With rising T the donors get ionised, and EF = Ec − kT ln(Nc/Nd) moves downward; at very high T (when ni ≫ Nd) intrinsic carriers dominate and EF approaches the intrinsic level Ei at mid-gap, and the material behaves as intrinsic.

Extrinsic – p-type: at 0 K, EF lies midway between Ev and acceptor level Ea. With increasing T, EF = Ev + kT ln(Nv/Na) moves upward towards Ei and finally reaches mid-gap at high temperature. Therefore the Fermi level of an extrinsic semiconductor moves toward the middle of the gap as temperature increases, and moves toward Ec (n-type) or Ev (p-type) with increasing doping.

rubric.point: Definition of direct band gap semiconductor (same k for CB minimum and VB maximum)
Definition of indirect band gap semiconductor (different k, phonon needed)
Correct E–k diagrams for both with vertical/non-vertical transitions
Examples (direct: GaAs, GaN, InP; indirect: Si, Ge, GaP)
Consequences/applications (LED, laser vs. Si transistors/solar cells)

answer: E–k diagram. In a crystal the energy of an electron is a function of its wave-vector k (crystal momentum p = ħk). The conduction band has an energy minimum Ec and the valence band has a maximum Ev; the band gap Eg = Ec − Ev.

Direct band gap semiconductor. The minimum of the conduction band and the maximum of the valence band occur at the same value of k (usually k = 0). An electron can drop from the conduction band to the valence band (or be excited) with no change in momentum – a vertical transition on the E–k diagram – by emitting (absorbing) a photon whose energy hν = Eg. The photon's momentum (h/λ ~ 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s) is negligible compared with the crystal momentum. Examples: GaAs, InP, GaN, InAs, CdS, CdTe.

Indirect band gap semiconductor. The conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum occur at different values of k. A transition between them needs a change in crystal momentum which a photon cannot supply, so a third particle – a phonon (lattice vibration) – must be emitted or absorbed simultaneously, to conserve momentum and energy. Such a three-body process is much less probable. Examples: Si (Eg = 1.12 eV), Ge (0.67 eV), GaP, AlAs.

Consequences. Direct materials have a high probability of radiative recombination and strong light absorption, which makes them suitable for LEDs, laser diodes, and thin-film solar cells (GaAs, CdTe). Indirect materials have longer carrier lifetimes and mostly non-radiative recombination, so they are poor light emitters; silicon is used in integrated circuits, transistors and bulk solar cells but not in LEDs.
formulas: Direct: k<sub>c,min</sub> = k<sub>v,max</sub>; Indirect: k<sub>c,min</sub> ≠ k<sub>v,max</sub>

(b) Indirect: valence band maximum at k = 0, conduction band minimum shifted to k = k₀; a slanted transition with a photon (vertical) plus a phonon (horizontal) arrow.

rubric.point: V–I characteristic of LED (1st quadrant, forward bias, light emission)
V–I characteristic of photodiode (reverse bias, 3rd quadrant, photocurrent ∝ intensity)
V–I characteristic of solar cell (4th quadrant, power generation) with diagram of all three
Distinction between photoelectric and photovoltaic effects (two or more points)

answer: LED (forward bias, light emitter). The V–I curve is that of a diode in the first quadrant: negligible current below the knee voltage (1.8–3.3 V depending on colour) and then a rapid exponential rise. Electrical power is converted into light; no light in reverse bias.

Photodiode (reverse bias, light detector). Operated in the third quadrant with reverse bias. In the dark, only the small reverse saturation current (dark current) flows; under illumination the reverse current increases in proportion to the light intensity (I = I₀ + Iph), giving nearly horizontal, equally spaced curves for increasing intensity. It consumes power from the supply; used as a light sensor.

Solar cell (no bias, power source). Under illumination the diode curve is shifted down by IL and passes through the fourth quadrant, cutting the voltage axis at Voc and the current axis at −Isc. In this quadrant V × I is negative in the diode convention, i.e. the device delivers power to the load. The photodiode may be treated as the solar cell operated in the third quadrant (photoconductive mode).

Comparison. LED – forward bias, converts electricity to light, I–V in 1st quadrant. Photodiode – reverse bias (or zero bias), converts light into current signal, 3rd quadrant, current proportional to light. Solar cell – no external bias, converts light into electrical power, 4th quadrant, large area, optimised for Pmax.

Photoelectric effect vs photovoltaic effect. (i) The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a (metal) surface when light of frequency above a threshold frequency ν₀ falls on it (hν = φ + ½mv²max); electrons leave the material (external effect). (ii) The photovoltaic effect is the generation of an emf (voltage) across a p–n junction when light with hν ≥ Eg creates electron–hole pairs that are separated by the built-in field; the carriers remain within the material (internal effect). The photoelectric effect needs an external collecting electrode/vacuum and typically UV; the photovoltaic effect produces voltage by itself, without any applied bias, in visible light.
